st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s account of competence risk and user-dependent gains with two large randomized learning experiments. It distinguishes immediate AI-assisted output from durable skill acquisition, finds larger learning gains among stronger baseline learners, and shows that information and feedback can improve independent practice—supporting deliberate scaffolding rather than tool access alone.
qs: However, these benefits are unevenly distributed; students with      higher baseline proficiency gain more from AI, suggesting that AI acts as an amplifier in skill-acquisition      contexts.
We find that both AI disclosure and AI feedback      improve score gains and stimulate independent practice.

st.t: Skill gaps: Assisted equality can hide learning divides
st.an: The source directly supports the distinction between assisted task performance and durable skill acquisition, while materially extending it with randomized field evidence that AI coaching improved writing and independent practice but delivered larger gains to learners with higher baseline proficiency. It also identifies information disclosure, feedback and tailored scaffolding as ways to improve learning without simply increasing AI usage, although absorptive capacity remains a theoretical explanation rather than an experimentally isolated mechanism.
qs: AI may act as an equalizer when the output is the endpoint, but it may act as an amplifier when learning and skill acquisition are the endpoint.
This finding indicates that rather than serving as a skill equalizer, AI acts as an amplifier; the performance premium is significantly more pronounced for students with higher baseline proficiency.

kp.k: Skill acquisition differs fundamentally from AI-assisted task completion
kp.d: This SSRN working paper by Ting Hou, Renee Rui Chen and Yinliang Tan, identified in the supplied metadata as deposited with Crossref on 29 July 2026, examines IELTS writing education rather than legal practice. The authors contrast earlier task-completion research, including legal reasoning studies, with learning settings: producing a usable AI-assisted artifact can substitute for missing competence, whereas acquiring skills requires learners to absorb and internalize feedback. They propose this distinction as a boundary condition for claims that AI equalizes performance.
qs: But these findings may not generalize to settings, such as learning, where the goal is not artifact production, but skill acquisition.
The student must absorb, evaluate, and internalize whatever the AI generates.
AI may act as an equalizer when the output is the endpoint, but it may act as an amplifier when learning and skill acquisition are the endpoint.

kp.k: AI coaching scaffolds writing while preserving independent practice
kp.d: The experiments took place on an unnamed Asian IELTS preparation platform serving more than 300,000 registered users. Its AI Coaching Assistant divides essay writing into outlining, introduction, topic sentences, paragraph expansion and conclusion, with diagnostic feedback and linguistic guidance throughout. Students can instead compose complete essays independently. The platform's identity is withheld under a non-disclosure agreement.
qs: Serving more than 300,000 registered users, the digital platform delivers a comprehensive IELTS preparation ecosystem
The students also retain the option to practice independently, composing essays in their entirety without reliance on AI-based interventions, to ensure learning autonomy.
The platform’s name is omitted due to a non-disclosure agreement.

kp.k: Randomized AI access improved writing scores
kp.d: Study 1 randomly assigned 13,806 newly registered students to AI access or legacy independent exercises: 8,212 received access and 5,594 were controls. Mean writing score gains on a 9-point scale were 0.92 versus 0.69, described by the authors as a 33.3% increase. Table 3 reports an intent-to-treat coefficient of 0.239 (standard error 0.006; p < 0.01). Score gain is the endline score minus the registration diagnostic baseline.
qs: The platform randomly assigns 13,806 newly registered students to either a treatment or a control group.
Students with access to the AI assistant achieve an average score gain of 0.92
representing a 33.3% increase.
the coefficient of AI represents the intent-to-treat effect of the AI on student score gain relative to the omitted control group.

kp.k: AI access increased independent writing practice
kp.d: In Study 1, students with AI access completed 25.17 independent writing tasks on average versus 20.15 among controls, a reported 24.9% increase. The adjusted effect was 5.03 additional tasks (p < 0.01). Engagement intensity counts completed and submitted independent writing tasks, not AI-assisted exercises; it therefore measures autonomous practice rather than tool invocation frequency. The authors interpret the increase as consistent with coaching sustaining motivation and making practice more manageable.
qs: They also complete 25.17 inde- pendent writing sessions on average, compared with 20.15 sessions in the control group, representing a 24.9% increase.
Notably, this metric excludes exercises performed with the help of AI tools, thereby serving as a direct proxy for the student’s autonomous effort and investment in the learning process.
the coefficient of AI remains positive and statistically significant (β = 5.03, p < 0.01).

kp.k: Higher-proficiency learners benefited more from AI access
kp.d: Study 1 reports positive interactions between AI access and baseline writing score for score gain (β = 0.031, p < 0.01) and independent practice (β = 0.65, p < 0.05). The authors interpret these findings through absorptive capacity theory: prior knowledge helps learners recognize useful feedback and convert suggestions into writing strategies. They describe AI as amplifying initial ability in this setting, rather than helping lower-performing students catch up. Most other examined demographic and background characteristics did not significantly moderate the effects.
qs: For score gain, the interaction between AI and Baseline Score is positive and statistically significant (β = 0.031, p < 0.01).
The interaction between AI and Baseline Score is also positive and statistically significant (β = 0.65, p < 0.05).
Together, these findings suggest a complementarity between AI coaching and students’ writing ability.

Most of these characteristics, including age, regional economy, prior exam attempts, and target score, do not significantly moder- ate the effect of AI access on either score gain or engagement intensity.

kp.k: Study 2 randomized disclosure and feedback framing
kp.d: Study 2 assigned 8,868 newly registered students to nine combinations of pre-use disclosure and post-use feedback, with AI access available to everyone. The reported experimental period was May 7, 2025, to August 7, 2025. Disclosure conditions were none, functionality and effectiveness; feedback conditions were none, mastery through personal score improvement and performance through relative ranking. The effectiveness message stated that the tool had helped 289,346 users achieve an average writing score improvement of 1.1 points; this was the intervention's communicated claim.

kp.k: Disclosure improved scores and independently completed practice
kp.d: Across Study 2, mean score gains were 0.85 without disclosure and 0.88 under both functionality and effectiveness disclosure. Table 5 reports full-sample adjusted effects of 0.03 points for each disclosure type. The authors describe effectiveness disclosure as more robust across feedback conditions, although Table A2 reports no significant overall score-gain difference between the disclosure types (p = 0.58). Independent practice averaged 20.85, 23.46 and 26.48 sessions respectively; Table 7 reports adjusted increases of 2.50 and 5.46 sessions relative to no disclosure (both p < 0.01).
qs: These results suggest that both disclosure types improve student outcomes and effectiveness disclosure appears more robust across feedback conditions.

the mean engagement intensity under the non-disclosure condition is 20.85 times, which is significantly lower than the 23.46 times under the functionality disclosure condition (p < 0.01) and the 26.48 times under the effectiveness disclosure condition (p < 0.01).

kp.k: Both feedback types improved outcomes among AI adopters
kp.d: The Study 2 feedback analysis is restricted to 6,408 students who adopted AI coaching, because feedback followed adoption. Mean score gains were 0.96 without feedback, 1.00 with mastery feedback and 0.99 with performance feedback; adjusted increases were 0.04 and 0.03 points respectively (both p < 0.01). Independent practice averaged 21.18, 28.40 and 27.73 sessions respectively, with adjusted increases of 7.26 and 6.57 sessions (both p < 0.01). The paper supports benefits from both feedback conditions rather than a clear overall superiority of mastery: reported pairwise differences between mastery and performance were not significant for scores or practice.
qs: We next examine the impact of feedback mechanisms on student per- formance among the 6, 408 students who adopted the AI coaching tool.
As feedback is only available post-adoption, our analysis restricts the sample to these adopters to isolate the effect of the inter- vention.
Students in the no feedback group achieved an average score increase of 0.96.
students in the mastery feedback and performance feedback groups exhibited higher gains of 1.00 and 0.99, respectively.

kp.k: Effectiveness disclosure and mastery feedback reinforced independent practice
kp.d: The adopter-sample interaction analysis reports an additional 3.38 independent practice sessions for effectiveness disclosure combined with mastery feedback (standard error 1.16; p < 0.01). Other engagement interaction terms were not significant. The authors interpret this as complementary expectation-setting and reinforcement of individual progress. Table 8 labels its first outcome Score Gain and reports no significant score-gain interactions, although the accompanying prose and column-description note refer to AI usage.
qs: The interaction coefficient for Ef f ectiveness × M astery is positive and highly significant (3.38, p < 0.01).
In contrast, the remaining interaction terms show no statistically significant impact.
the motivational framing of AI feedback and the signaling of tool value do not operate in isolation; rather, they function as a complementary design bundle.

kp.k: Learning improvements did not require greater AI usage
kp.d: Neither disclosure nor feedback produced a statistically significant change in total AI invocations. Mean usage was 25.42 without disclosure, 26.00 with functionality disclosure and 25.58 with effectiveness disclosure. Among the feedback-analysis sample, means were 35.68 without feedback, 35.47 with mastery and 35.41 with performance feedback. The authors describe the combination of improved scores and independent practice with unchanged usage volume as usage-outcome decoupling, and argue against treating tool-use frequency as the sole measure of educational value.
qs: We measure AI usage as the total number of times a student invoked the AI coaching tool during the experimental period.
These results suggest that different AI disclosure strategies do not alter the descriptive volume of students’ tool usage.
This pattern suggests a usage-outcome decoupling: the same AI tool, used at similar levels, can generate different learning outcomes depending on how the platform frames the learning experience.

kp.k: Robustness analyses retained the principal reported patterns
kp.d: Registration-date fixed effects retained positive effects of AI access, disclosure and feedback, as well as the positive interaction between baseline proficiency and AI access. In Study 1, the time-adjusted AI coefficients were 0.254 for score gain and 6.97 for independent practice. A separate analysis retained controls and only treatment students who used AI at least once, yielding 11,853 observations; it reported positive effects and a baseline-score interaction significant at p < 0.01 for score gain and p < 0.1 for engagement. These are the paper's reported robustness exercises, distinct from its primary intent-to-treat analysis.
qs: we re-estimate our main specifications by including registration time fixed effects.

kp.k: Authors recommend targeted scaffolding and evidence-based information design
kp.d: The authors recommend supplementary support for lower-proficiency students, including error-diagnosis drills and guided revision tutorials, to help them internalize AI feedback. They advise platforms to combine pre-use effectiveness information with post-use mastery feedback and to measure learning and independent practice rather than usage alone. They also recommend that policymakers encourage evidence-based disclosure for its operational as well as compliance value. These are recommendations arising from the education experiments, not tested interventions in legal training or legal services.
qs: Platforms should implement tailored scaffolding for students with lower baseline proficiency to ensure equitable learning outcomes.
such as error-diagnosis drills or guided revision tutorials

By adopting a two-channel communication strategy, that is, disclosing the AI’s effective- ness ex ante to build trust and providing mastery-oriented feedback ex post to reinforce progress, platforms can significantly improve AI outcomes.

Policymakers should encourage such dis- closure not only to satisfy regulatory standards but as a functional strategy to ensure that learners can effectively navigate and benefit from emerging AI technologies.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hou, Chen and Tan claim that AI coaching improves writing performance and independent practice, but benefits stronger learners disproportionately.
pts.d: This cross-domain source concerns IELTS preparation, not legal services. The authors report that access to a staged AI writing coach increases average writing score gains and the number of independent writing tasks completed. They argue that AI can amplify initial ability differences in skill acquisition because learners must interpret and internalize feedback, unlike task-completion settings where AI can substitute for missing competence. They also claim that pre-use disclosure and post-use feedback improve learning and independent practice without significantly increasing AI usage. They describe effectiveness disclosure as more influential than functionality disclosure, and report an additional engagement benefit from combining effectiveness disclosure with mastery feedback. Their proposed explanations emphasize absorptive capacity, motivation, confidence and expectations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors base their claims on two randomized field experiments, with 13,806 and 8,868 newly registered students respectively.
pts.d: Study 1 compares AI access with legacy independent writing exercises: 8,212 students receive access and 5,594 serve as controls. Reported mean score gains are 0.92 versus 0.69 on a nine-point scale, described as a 33.3% increase; independent practice averages 25.17 versus 20.15 tasks, a 24.9% increase. The adjusted intent-to-treat coefficients are 0.239 score points and 5.03 independent tasks (both p < 0.01). Interactions between AI access and baseline proficiency are 0.031 for score gain (p < 0.01) and 0.65 for independent practice (p < 0.05). Study 2 crosses three disclosure conditions with three feedback conditions. Table 5 reports overall score-gain coefficients of approximately 0.03 for each disclosure type, and 0.04 and 0.03 for mastery and performance feedback respectively; feedback analyses use 6,408 AI adopters. Table 7 reports independent-practice increases of 2.50 and 5.46 tasks for functionality and effectiveness disclosure, and 7.26 and 6.57 for mastery and performance feedback. The effectiveness-by-mastery interaction adds 3.38 independent tasks (p < 0.01). The authors offer registration-time fixed effects and an adopter-only analysis as robustness checks. Absorptive capacity and motivational theories provide their explanations for the observed patterns.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern outcomes during platform-based IELTS experiments, with Study 2 explicitly dated May 7–August 7, 2025; the central boundary condition is skill acquisition rather than output production.
pts.d: The supplied metadata identifies the source as a 2026 SSRN preprint. Study 2 runs for three months; a separate calendar period for Study 1 is not specified in the supplied text. Score gain measures endline minus baseline performance during the experiment. The authors frame the results as evidence about durable learning, but the reported measurements concern the experimental period rather than a specified long-term follow-up. The coach provides diagnostic feedback through five writing stages, and students retain the option to practice independently. Independent-practice counts exclude AI-assisted exercises. Study 2 gives all participants AI access; its feedback comparisons are restricted to users who adopt the tool. The authors condition the amplifier claim on learners needing sufficient prior knowledge to absorb and apply AI feedback. They do not supply a forecast date for wider adoption or effects in legal services.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source identifies IELTS learners, education-platform managers and policymakers as affected, with particular concern for learners with lower initial proficiency.
pts.d: The experiments involve newly registered students at an unnamed Asian education provider whose platform serves more than 300,000 registered users. Higher-proficiency learners receive larger learning and independent-practice benefits. The authors recommend supplementary scaffolding for lower-proficiency students, including error-diagnosis drills and guided revision tutorials, so they can better interpret and internalize feedback. For platform managers, they recommend treating disclosure and feedback as product-design features, combining effectiveness information before use with mastery-oriented feedback afterward, and measuring learning outcomes rather than relying on AI usage frequency. For policymakers, they advocate evidence-based disclosure as an operational aid to effective learning, not merely a compliance measure. These are recommendations derived from the experiments; the source does not report a separate test of the proposed scaffolding interventions or impacts on lawyers, legal clients or legal markets.
